prompt: You have reduced 3-SAT to a new decision problem in polynomial time, preserving both answers. What is still needed before calling the new problem NP-complete?

options.text: Prove it has no polynomial-time algorithm
options.explanation: That would resolve P versus NP, and is not part of an NP-completeness proof.

options.text: Show polynomial-size yes-certificates have a polynomial-time verifier
options.explanation: The reduction establishes NP-hardness; this separate argument establishes membership in NP.

options.text: Test that the solver is slow on several examples
options.explanation: Measurements on selected inputs do not establish the class membership required for NP-completeness.
Worst-case completeness does not require every input to be hard.

workedExample: The reduction transfers hardness: an algorithm for the new problem could solve the known NP-complete source. But hardness alone does not provide a short certificate or a verifier for the new problem. Establish those separately to conclude NP-completeness.

prompt: Which of these problems are known to be **NP-hard**? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: NP-hard (in fact NP-complete) by the Cook–Levin theorem.
NP-hard: any NP problem reduces to it by mapping x to a machine that halts iff x is a yes-instance. It is not in NP (it's undecidable), so it is NP-hard but not NP-complete.
2-SAT is in P (linear time via strongly connected components). It would be NP-hard only if P equals NP, which nobody believes.
NP-hard: it's an optimisation problem whose decision version is NP-complete. It isn't in NP itself because it isn't a yes/no problem.

options.text: Shortest path between two vertices with nonnegative weights
options.explanation: In P (Dijkstra). Like 2-SAT, it's not NP-hard unless P equals NP.

workedExample: SAT is NP-complete. For Halting, write a machine that decides the given NP instance, halts on yes and loops on no: writing that description is fast even if running it is slow. Optimising a TSP tour also solves its hard threshold decision version. In contrast, 2-SAT and nonnegative shortest-path decision are in P, so hardness for either would imply P equals NP.
